column16: Chicago adopted an updated Sustainable Development Policy (SDP) in December 2024 that sets minimum sustainability standards via a points-based system for City-assisted projects, explicitly promoting sustainable building methods and materials that decrease greenhouse gas emissions and improve public health. Projects approved after January 1, 2025 must comply with the 2024 SDP update, using either “Menu strategies” or a “Third-Party Certification + Menu” pathway. column16: The GLA Group annually procures around 9.5bn worth of products and services. The Mayor is committed to 'leading by example', using the scale and diversity of this public spending to improve the lives of Londoners, by creating a fairer and more environmentally sustainable city. (The GLA Group comprises City Hall, Transport for London, the Metropolitan Police, London Fire Brigade and the London Legacy Development Corporation). This is overseen by the GLA Group Responsible Procurement Policy, which includes an objective to enhance environmental impacts including whole-life carbon reduction. The GLA Group's Responsible Procurement Delivery Plan (2025-28) seeks to reduce supply chain emissions by requiring suppliers of contracts over £5m to produce emissions Carbon Reduction Statements,; identify carbon-reduction and climate resilience opportunities in carbon-intensive contracts; and reducing emissions from suppliers' plant equipment and vehicle deliveries. The Climate and Equalities Tool (the C&E Tool) has been developed by GLA staff in collaboration with staff at the University of Manchester Tyndall Centre's Centre for Climate Change and Social Transformations. The C&E Tool is a simple excel tool that staff are encouraged to use at the start of a new project. It shows the user how to assess the potential climate and equalities impacts of their work, and helps them to strengthen these or avoid unintended negative consequences during project development. The C&E Tool is designed to be applicable to all types and scales of projects, including procurement programmes. The Climate and Equalities teams also provide support, guidance and review to users across the GLA. The C&E Tool has been shared with other functional bodies in the GLA Group, as well as some boroughs and partners. We have published a generalised, public version of the C&E Tool for boroughs and partners https://data.london.gov.uk/dataset/climate---equalities-tool.

Environmental requirements must always be imposed in purchasing and procurement where justified and should aim to achieve the goals of the City Environment Programme. In addition, in several categories of purchases, the City is such a large purchaser that there are good opportunities to influence the supplier market in a certain direction, which also benefits other consumers. For procured transport services, many recent agreements state 100% renewable fuels as a requirement. The City also co-operates with other local, regional and national actors to align the requirements in order to push the suppliers. One tool the City uses is category-based purchasing, in which the City analyzes both the city's aggregated needs and purchasing patterns and the markets to gain better knowledge before procurement. This is also a way to train the many procurers in the City organisation.Other measures taken are that the City requires information on the total carbon footprint of new buildings, minimizes business travel by air and sets climate requirements for the purchase of food and meals in the City's operations. The foundations are laid down in the City's Purchase Programme.

Procurement is continuing to ensure it is aligned to wider Council objectives and a key priority is to evolve our approach to Social Value and also to embed Climate and Ethical Procurement considerations within Commissioning and Procurement practice. The aim is to maximise every pound spent to benefit the residents and businesses of Essex and to support the organisational goal of reaching net zero by 2030. Essex County Council spends over £1.2bn per annum on goods, services and capital projects in order to run its operations. Working with the Carbon Trust, ECC has baselined these (Scope 3) emissions produced under our Purchased Goods & Services and Capital Goods. ECC has set out a procurement action plan, to gain more detailed measurements, incentivise reduction of emissions and to support our suppliers to understand, set and reach their own climate targets. To date ECC has achieved:•Inclusion of a requirement for climate to be considered in all tenders over £100,000, This may result in the supplier providing a Carbon Reduction Plan (CRP) which meets the requirements of central government's Procurement Policy Note 06/21. To lead by example, ECC will be producing an organisational CRP in line with these requirements. •We take account of Social Value when awarding most contracts. Social Value includes climate measures used to ensure that environmental benefits are taken into account when deciding which bid is successful. These measures have been updated for 2024. These benefit suppliers who support Circular Economy solutions through their supply chains, as well as reducing waste and monitoring fleet emissions. 
•Developing climate transition plans for our key emitting categories (Passenger Transport, Highways, Waste, Nursing & Residential Care, Homecare Services and Facilities Management & Property), as identified in our supplier emissions report. The procurement team will be working with service commissioners to understand the current context of their markets, what legislation will be impactful to drive climate action, key climate targets already in place and contract renewal dates. This will enable each category, or indeed contract, to have a specific action plan to reduce emissions throughout the life of the contracts, ideally by baselining contract specific emissions and allowing prospective suppliers to bid against reducing these. 
•Continuing to baseline contract specific emissions and develop measures to ensure that emissions are reduced throughout the contractual terms, where appropriate. Working with our suppliers, we are creating measurement tools specific to their market sector, running webinars and publishing information to support suppliers' understanding and transition to net zero. 
•Our supplier sustainability charter is being updated with clear targets in the environmental section and our procurement policy is being amended in line with ECC's wider ambitions. •A new environmental policy is being produced. This will cover buying standards as well as expectations for how the organisation meets the climate challenge. 
•Measurement of further Scope 3 emissions (Upstream and Downstream Transportation and Distribution, Waste Generated in Operations, Business Travel and Employee Commuting) will enable us to publish our own Carbon Reduction Plan for these key areas. https://www.essex.gov.uk/sites/default/files/2024-05/Procurement%20Strategy%20-%20April%202024.pdf

column16:
Yes, Manchester City Council (MCC) has a comprehensive strategy and set of standards aimed at reducing emissions from its procurement and purchasing activities. These are embedded within the Council's Climate Change Action Plan (CCAP) 2025-2030 that will be published in October 2025 and supported by practical tools, training, and supplier engagement initiatives.

Key Strategic Actions and Standards
1. Scope 3 Emissions Baseline and Reduction Planning
a. The Council is currently working
towards a full Scope 3 carbon footprint for the Council, including detailed analysis of
emissions from purchased goods and services.
b. This work includes prioritisation of Scope 3 categories for decarbonisation and the
development of targeted interventions and action plans.
2. Procurement Weightings and Supplier Requirements
a. All MCC tenders include a 10% weighting specifically for environmental impact, separate
from the 20% social value weighting.
b. Suppliers are required to provide carbon reduction plans (and when they don't have such
plan, provide an overview of how they are planning to reduce their carbon emissions in
the duration of their contracts) and baseline data, enabling MCC to assess and monitor
emissions during contract delivery.
3. Zero Carbon Toolkit and Training
a. MCC has developed a Zero Carbon Toolkit for Commissioners and Contract Managers,
which provides practical guidance on embedding environmental requirements throughout
the commissioning cycle—from need definition to contract management (please see
attached).
b. An e-learning module has been rolled out to support staff in understanding and applying
zero carbon principles in procurement. Further workshops will be delivered in September
and November that will offer a focused recap of the Zero Carbon Toolkit in Commissioning and Procurement, reinforcing the key concepts, tools, and methodologies that support environmentally responsible decision-making across the
commissioning cycle.
4. Contract Management and KPI Monitoring
a. Environmental KPIs are embedded in contracts and tracked via the Council's contract
management system (Atamis), supporting performance monitoring and Scope 3
reporting.
5. Supplier Engagement and Circular Economy
a. MCC works with suppliers, including SMEs and VCFSEs, to support carbon reduction
and circular economy practices.
b. A supplier toolkit is being developed in partnership with the Growth Company to help
suppliers understand and meet sustainability expectations. This is expected to be
launched in autumn.
6. CCAP 2025-2030 Commitments. The Council's CCAP includes specific procurement actions such as:
a. Maximising the impact of environmental weighting in tenders.
b. Embedding zero carbon priorities in service design and contract specifications.
c. Monitoring supplier performance on environmental KPIs.
d. Promoting sustainable materials and reducing single-use plastics.

Key objectives are to increase local and low-carbon production, reduce the consumption of high carbon products, encourage more low carbon cooking and meals and to reduce local waste and link all remaining waste to energy, composting and a circular economy. These objectives each have a series of actions to realise them.

Nottingham's Green Partnership formed in 1992 and is now made up of over 30 organisations across Nottingham, including large and small businesses, public sector organisations, the third sector and both universities. The organisations are working together to tackle the city's environmental challenges and to minimise its environmental impact. 

Some examples from across Nottingham:

final-commercial-and-procurement-strategy-2025-29-version-71.pdf Nottingham City Council's Procurement Strategy (2025 - 2029) aims to maximise local spend ensuring local growth and job creation. The newly implemented strategy prioritises sustainable and fair procurement as one of it's key aims. To achieve this, it aims to set appropriate carbon emissions reduction requirements in tenders, ask suppliers to submit their carbon emissions data and a carbon reduction plan, and to consider holding carbon footprint and target setting workshops for smaller suppliers alongside a phased introduction of tender requirements over time. The policy also sets out to identify areas of climate risk in their supply chains and ask contractors to tell them how they will manage possible risks arising due to extreme weather and climate change. Finally, it looks to minimise any negative environmental impacts of procuring goods, services and works through considering impacts to air quality and climate change, resource efficiency, waste reduction, and product lifespan.

187637.pdf Nottingham Trent University has received the Silver 'Food for Life' award, recognising the sustainable sourcing of ingredients in their catering (22% local, 72% UK-based, and 11% organic). Yes. 
English version of the City of Oslo's procurement strategy, politically adopted in 2017: https://sustainable-procurement.org/fileadmin/templates/sp_platform/lib/sp_platform_resources/tools/push_resource_file.php?uid=71f3f1e2
A number of processes have been initiated to reduce emissions resulting from the municipality's procurements. The municipality has developed a guide for reduced and smarter use of plastic in procurements, along with a guide to the circular economy in procurements. The latter explains how the municipal entities can contribute to sustainable and reduced consumption through measures such as prioritising reuse, repair and upgrading over new purchases. 
Oslo has an Action plan for sustainable, healthy and more plant-based food in the City of Oslo. The main objective of the action plan is that the City of Oslo's food consumption contributes to good public health and animal welfare, while indirect greenhouse gas emissions and negative impacts on the environment and society is significantly reduced. One of the goals in the action plan is to develop the supplier market for sustainable food and emphasize animal welfare and working conditions through the procurement and consumption of food and drink.
The City of Oslo has adopted standard climate and environmental requirements for procurement of transport (in procurements of goods and services) and procurements of building and construction sites. Both of these standard requirements were revised in 2025, and will be translated into English in the near future. The former standard requirements from 2019 are available in the links below. 
* Standard requirements transport (2019): https://www.klimaoslo.no/collection/standard-climate-and-environmental-requirements-for-transport-for-the-city-of-oslos-goods-and-services-procurements/ 

* Standard requirements building and construction sites (2019): https://www.klimaoslo.no/rapport/climate-requirements-construction-sites/ 

The revised standard requirements for transport, building and construction adopted in 2025, follows up market development and increases the focus on emission-free solutions, both for vehicles and machinery. Emission free machines are now the minimum requirement. 85% of energy use on our building and construction sites was emission free in 2024. 
We are currently working on increasing the scope to include embodied emissions from building and construction materials. 
Regarding social and ethical procurement practices: 
The City of Oslo continues to be at the forefront fighting work-related crime, and ensuring decent labour conditions for workers in our domestic and global supply chains. In 2017 the City of Oslo adopted the Oslo Model - a comprehensive framework of measures and requirements to help combat social dumping and to promote decent working conditions, using public procurement as a strategic tool. The model was revised and adopted in May 2023. One of the main changes is requirements for suppliers to work with due diligence for responsible business conduct, included in global supply chains. 
There is high risk of human rights breeches in many categories, among them, batteries and ICT-equipments, food and beverages and textiles. 
Another key instrument to work towards fair procurements, beside standard criteria, is use of fair labels certifications. 
The City of Oslo is a Fairtrade-city. A Steering Committee comprised of representatives from the municipality, business enterprises and NGOs is established and is taking actions to promote fair trade in the central functions of the city, including in procurement, and among the citizens. The most important step in this area in the past few years is the joint agreements in the food sector combined with category management to increase the share of fairtrade certified goods. 
More info on procurement practices and indicators is outlined in the different categories of goods and services listed above. Indicators for Scope 3 emissions from procurement are available here (this will be updated with improved calculations due to a newly purchased emissions calculator and a current project on data quality): https://www.klimaoslo.no/klimabarometeret/indirekte-utslipp/indirekte-utslipp-fra-kommunens-innkjop/ (in Norwegian)

The City of Portland has a sustainable procurement policy and program, attached. 
https://www.portland.gov/procurement/sustainable-procurement-program

The City of Portland's 2016 Sustainable Supply Chain Analysis identified construction services as the top spend category contributing to the City's supply chain greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Within construction services, concrete is one of the most GHG-intensive materials typically used on City construction projects. As a result, in 2019, after gathering both internal and external stakeholder input, the City established its Low-Carbon Concrete Initiative to reduce the overall carbon intensity of the concrete mixes used on City projects. From 2019 to early 2022, the Initiative involved: 1) establishing a product-specific Environmental Product Declaration (EPD) requirement for concrete mixes used on City projects; 2) conducting pilot tests of lower-embodied carbon concrete mixes; and 3) defining Global Warming Potential (GWP) Thresholds for concrete mixes. Based on the same supply chain analysis we also piloted warm mix asphalt: https://www.portlandoregon.gov/brfs/article/368274

A variety of our case studies on sustainable procurement can be found here: https://www.portlandoregon.gov/brfs/article/368274

Regarding vehicle and fuel purchasing, the fleet procurement team is incorporating a carbon shadow price into lifecycle cost assessments for new vehicles, which supports accelerated adoption of EV and alternative fuel vehicles.

column16: The City of Melbourne's ESG Procurement Framework embeds environmental, social and governance principles into every purchasing decision, with a strong focus on reducing carbon emissions. All staff involved in procurement are expected to apply these principles, ensuring every purchase considers its environmental impact across the full lifecycle of goods and services. The framework requires the use of positive and negative screening, where suppliers must declare any associations with harmful industries such as fossil fuels, and preference is given to those demonstrating low-carbon operations, renewable energy use, sustainable materials, and circular economy practices. To reinforce this commitment, a mandatory 10% weighting for ESG is applied in all procurement processes, ensuring sustainability and emissions reduction are consistently factored into decision making. This approach makes carbon-conscious procurement business as usual at the City of Melbourne and supports Council's target of achieving net zero emissions by 2040. Sustainability is also actively managed through our Supplier Relationship Management (SRM) program, where we work closely with suppliers to deliver the best long-term environmental outcomes.

Circular Procurement:

Circular procurement is widely recognized as a key urban policy lever to achieve waste reduction and sustainable consumption goals by leveraging public sector spending to increase the supply of innovative goods and services. The City of Toronto developed a Circular Procurement Framework and Implementation Plan in 2018 to support its efforts to transition to a circular economy. The Framework outlines how circular economy principles will be applied to the City's purchasing processes to drive waste reduction, economic growth, and social prosperity. Implementing circular procurement will advance the City's efforts to maximize the value of existing resources and reduce waste. This, in turn, help reduce GHG emissions and move the City closer to achieving its TransformTO' s goals.

Circular Procurement Implementation Plan and Framework: https://www.toronto.ca/legdocs/mmis/2018/gm/bgrd/backgroundfile-115664.pdf

On May 30, 2023, the City has awarded RFP 3743044527 to Sysco Toronto for the supply and delivery of groceries for Seniors Services and Long-Term Care Division, Shelter Support and Housing Administration Division and Children's Services Division (2023.GG4.20). During the RFP process, existing public procurement documents from the City were modified to incorporate the Cool Food Pledge requirement in measuring and quantifying emissions associated with the City's food procurement. The scoring criteria to evaluate proposals from potential Vendors also incorporated the Cool Food Pledge requirement.

https://secure.toronto.ca/council/agenda-item.do?item=2023.GG4.20

Recent updates and future directions:

Review of Procurement Bylaw:Toronto's Procurement Bylaw was reviewed in 2023, with amendments taking effect on July 1, 2024.
Policy updates:Revisions to the Procurement Processes Policy and the Social Procurement Policy are underway to align with the bylaw amendments and the TransformTO strategy.
Future reports:The Chief Procurement Officer is expected to report back in the first quarter of 2025 with further updates on how the procurement process can advance TransformTO objectives.
Toronto Green Standard: An update to the Toronto Green Standard, including revised greenhouse gas emission limits, is targeted for the fourth quarter of 2025, after the second phase of the Net Zero Transition Study is completed, according to the City of Toronto.

Key aspects of the policy:

Encouraging an Environmentally Responsible Procurement :The policy encourages bidders to offer environmentally preferred products and services, which are defined as those that are more energy-efficient, water-efficient, reduce waste, and minimize environmental impact.
Integrating environmental criteria: The policy aims to incorporate environmental performance criteria into supply chain procedures and processes.
Considering life-cycle costs: Environmentally responsible procurement considers the total cost of ownership, including environmental impacts over the product's entire life cycle.
Alignment with City goals: The ERP policy supports the city's broader environmental objectives, such as the TransformTO Net Zero Strategy, which aims to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
Focus on waste reduction and the circular economy: The policy is also viewed as a means to advance waste reduction and promote the circular economy, aligning with the provincial goal of a waste-free future.

Specific actions:
1. The Government has all along led by example by adopting green procurement for implementation of the concept of environmental protection. The Government's Stores and Procurement Regulations require bureaux and departments (B/Ds) to take environmental factors into consideration in drawing up tender specifications, so as to allow for fair competition of compliant products and services on a cost-effective basis, thereby promoting green procurement while ensuring the prudent use of public funds. 

Having regard to the practices and standards generally adopted in the market, the Government has developed a set of green specifications and guidelines for the products and services commonly used by the Government, so that B/Ds may practise green procurement in accordance with the relevant specifications. The Government reviews the green procurement list and relevant specifications from time to time to keep abreast of the latest market development and the procurement needs of B/Ds. In July 2021, the Government expanded the green procurement list from 150 to 183 items, updating the specifications for each product and providing additional tips for green procurement. In February 2024, the Government updated the green procurement circular to set electric vehicles as the standard for the procurement or replacement of all government private cars as far as possible. Recently, the Government further updated the green specifications for the procurement of LED lamps with motion sensor function and filtered water dispensers. In 2024, the Government procured green products and services with a total value of $8.42 billion, which is an increase of about 19.3% as compared to $7.06 billion in 2023. The Government will continue to promote green procurement by disseminating the latest green procurement list, relevant specifications, tips and both local and international best practices online for public reference.


2. The Environmental Protection Department is using the electronic procurement system to handle the quotation exercises. The Environmental Protection Department also adopts the electronic tendering system for processing tendering matters and receiving electronic submission of offer. The subject teams of the Environmental Protection Department are required to adopt the green procurement practice with details as stipulated in the Environment Bureau Circular Memorandum No. 1/2021.

Following a first public procurement scheme from 2016 to 2020, the Paris City Council adopted a new responsible public procurement scheme (SPASER) in December 2021. With 1.6 billion euros in annual public contracts and a total turnover of over 1.4 billion euros per year for concession contracts an ambitious responsible purchasing policy is an important lever to promote social inclusion social and solidarity economy (SSE) and to meet the ecological transition commitments outlined in the City's Climate Plan. This includes aiming for 75% and 50% of contracts respectively incorporating provisions favorable to the circular economy and biodiversity. 
(https://cdn.paris.fr/paris/2021/12/20/3acce5e0b9de3a605f0a1ef85fd4a5fc.pdf)

In addition to its SPASER, the City of Paris conducts a yearly climate assessment of the local government budget by public policy. The climate assessment of the City of Paris budget is based on a methodology developed by the Institute for Climate Economics (I4CE) It categorizes the operating and investment expenses of the local government based on their impact favorable unfavorable neutral or undefined on greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions mitigation. First conducted in 2020 for the 2019 financial statement the climate assessment has been carried out annually since then. The results are published each year on Paris.fr in the financial report of the previous years financial statement. The climate assessment for the 2024 financial statement was conducted on an analysis scope of €8,215 million. Expenses that are strictly financial remain excluded from the analysis scope. 

The results obtained in 2024 confirm the trends observed in previous years. According to the methodology, a significant proportion of expenses are classified as neutral in terms of GHG emissions mitigation 79,6%. A continued reduction in the share of expenses with an undefined impact decreasing from 17.2% in 2020 to 2,3% in 2022. This phenomenon can be explained with an increase of positive impact projects and a shift of certain operational costs (such as the City 100% renewable electricity contract).

In 2005, Chapter 2 of the San Francisco Environment Code set a comprehensive system for the City to identify, purchase, and use environmentally preferred products. This ordinance was strengthened by executive directive in 2008 and created the SF Approved service operated by the San Francisco Environment Department. SF Approved provides a list of products that have been screened for environmental benefits, cost, reduced toxicity, and performance. Categories include, but are not limited to, janitorial cleaners, office paper, disposable food containers and utensils, building supplies, furniture, electronics, lighting, and landscaping products. The City has also implemented a 'Green Technology Policy' that requires the Department of Environment to spend no less than 90% of purchase dollars on compliant technology products including personal computers, servers, imaging equipment, televisions and large displays. 

In 2024, San Francisco Environment Department began to work with its infrastructure agencies including SFO, Port, and Public Works to develop progressive design and construction standards. These standards will result in the reduction of embodied carbon starting with pilots on municipal vertical and non-vertical projects that encourage the procurement of low carbon materials whether sourced from existing building materials deconstructed and reused or, if new, assembled from low carbon materials such as for concrete. In 2025, Public Works' Bureau of Architects and Engineers are modifying master concrete specifications to be low carbon for both structural and non-structural concrete, hence forcing industry to provide low carbon concrete for all municipal projects.

1)시장은 「환경친화적 자동차의 개발 및 보급 촉진에 관한 법률」에서 정의한 ▲전기자동차 ▲태양광자동차 ▲수소전기자동차 등 친환경차를 우선적으로 구매해야 합니다.
2)창원시는 행정기관, 공공기관, 산하 기관 차량도 신규 또는 교체 시 친환경차 도입을 원칙으로 하고, 친환경차 공급 확대에 적극 노력해야 합니다.
3)이 조항은 공공부문의 모범적 역할을 통해 민간 부문으로의 저탄소차량 보급 확대도 유도한다는 정책적 의미를 가집니다.

<연계 정책 및 이행내용>
1)창원시는 해당 조례와 연동해 매년 전기차·수소차, 충전 인프라 보급사업을 적극 추진하고 있으며, 2025년에도 다수의 전기차, 수소차, 충전소 지원사업을 실시 중입니다.
2)“친환경차 의무구매 조항”은 모든 공공조달, 구매사업 정책의 필수 준수사항입니다.
3)즉, 창원시의 친환경차 우선 구매·보급은 조례에 명확히 규정된 행정책임이며, 시장은 법적 근거를 토대로 친환경차 확대와 온실가스 저감의 이행 주체 역할을 수행해야 합니다.

Ankara Metropolitan Municipality (ABB) has recognized that procurement and purchasing processes represent one of the most powerful levers available to local governments for driving systemic change toward low-carbon, resource-efficient, and socially responsible economic development. While the direct greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions of municipal operations are significant, the indirect emissions embedded in purchased goods, contracted services, outsourced infrastructure, and long-term supply agreements are often several times larger. For this reason, ABB has formally integrated sustainable procurement principles into its climate strategy, aligning with the guidance of the Global Covenant of Mayors (GCoM), the European Commission's Green Public Procurement framework, and best practices from ICLEI's Procura+ network.

The Sustainable Procurement Guidelines adopted by ABB are designed to reduce the carbon intensity of municipal purchases while also delivering multiple co-benefits such as cost savings, improved health outcomes, local job creation, and enhanced transparency. The approach is comprehensive, spanning the entire procurement cycle—from needs assessment and tender preparation, to supplier evaluation, contract management, and post-contract performance monitoring.

Key elements of the strategy include:

Life-Cycle Costing and Emission Accounting:
Rather than focusing solely on the upfront purchase price, ABB evaluates bids based on life-cycle costs, including acquisition, energy use, maintenance, and end-of-life disposal. This methodology incorporates the carbon footprint of materials and services, encouraging bidders to demonstrate how their products minimize embedded emissions. For example, in construction projects, tender documents explicitly request information on embodied carbon in cement and steel, incentivizing suppliers who can provide certified low-carbon alternatives.

Priority Sectors:
ABB has identified high-impact categories where procurement choices can deliver significant GHG reductions:

Construction materials: Prioritizing recycled aggregates, low-carbon concrete, and sustainable timber.

Transportation: Requiring low-emission vehicles in municipal fleets and mandating Euro 6 or electric buses in public transport tenders.

Energy supply: Procuring renewable electricity through power purchase agreements and ensuring municipal buildings progressively transition to 100% clean energy.

ICT and electronics: Applying “right to repair” principles, energy efficiency criteria, and end-of-life recycling obligations for purchased IT equipment.

Cleaning services and chemicals: Favoring biodegradable, non-toxic cleaning products to minimize both emissions and public health risks.

Supplier Engagement and Capacity Building:
ABB acknowledges that small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) form the backbone of the local economy, and that strict sustainability requirements can pose challenges. Therefore, ABB provides technical guidance, workshops, and pre-tender consultations to suppliers. This ensures that sustainability criteria are transparent and achievable, while also motivating suppliers to invest in innovation and align with low-carbon business models.

Verification and Standards:
Where possible, ABB requires suppliers to certify compliance with internationally recognized sustainability standards. For carbon-related criteria, this includes ISO 14064 GHG accounting standards, Environmental Product Declarations (EPDs), and eco-labels recognized by the EU. Verification mechanisms are embedded into contracts, and penalties are stipulated for non-compliance.

Social Co-Benefits and Fair Procurement:
Procurement is also used as a tool to promote equity and resilience. ABB's tenders give preference to suppliers who demonstrate social responsibility, such as fair labor practices, gender equality, and local employment. In particular, projects that support vulnerable groups or promote circular economy initiatives are given higher weighting. By linking climate action with social inclusion, ABB ensures that the benefits of the low-carbon transition are shared across communities.

Monitoring, Reporting, and Continuous Improvement:
All major procurement projects are tracked through ABB's internal climate governance system. Procurement officers must report on sustainability outcomes, including estimated GHG reductions, cost savings, and qualitative benefits. Lessons learned from each procurement cycle are integrated into future tenders, allowing for continuous refinement of criteria. ABB intends to publish annual procurement sustainability reports starting in 2025, providing transparency for citizens and accountability for suppliers.
Through its sustainable procurement strategy, ABB demonstrates leadership in aligning public spending with climate objectives. By systematically integrating life-cycle thinking, emissions accounting, supplier engagement, and verification mechanisms.

The City of Cape Town (the City) has a long history of implementing green procurement in its operations and large capital project. See the City's Global Lead City Network on Sustainable Procurement profile for a more detailed overview: https://glcn-on-sp.org/fileadmin/user_upload/Cape_Town/GLCN_city_profile_City_of_Cape_Town_2021.pdf. The City has committed to implementing green procurement in various high-level policies and strategies including, the Environmental, Resilience, Climate Change Strategy and Inclusive Economic Growth strategies as well as the Supply Chain Management Policy and adopted a Green Procurement Action Plan in 2020 to give effect to that commitment. 

The action plan defines a set of principles to guide green procurement decision-making, defines a set of desired objectives and outcomes, and lay out the specific actions required to effectively transition towards green procurement in all of the City's operations and purchasing decisions, with the following objectives: 

• 1: Ensure that the City has in place appropriate policies to support green procurement, including associated administrative tools 
• 2: Maximise the City's sourcing and purchasing of sustainable products 
• 3: Maximise the City's sourcing and purchasing of sustainable services 
• 4: Increase the number of green/sustainable buildings built by the City, with a long-term aim of a complete transition to green/sustainable building 
• 5: Incorporate green procurement into the City's large capital projects 
• 6: Communicate effectively with the public, City contractors and City staff regarding green procurement 
• 7: Monitor and evaluate the City's performance in terms of green procurement 

During this reporting period (2024/25) the City continued implementation of short-medium term actions of the Green Procurement Action Plan. Priority Actions undertaken included: 
•	Continued to develop draft specifications for various material categories. 
•	In collaboration with the Sustainable Energy Markets) Department, Risk and Resilience Department, and the Urban Sustainability Unit, it was determined that a directive be developed for green new City buildings, aligned with the City's Net-Zero built environment commitments. Work is ongoing in this regard. 
•	Drafted sustainable design principles for various types of capital/infrastructure projects.
•	Continued drafting set of guidelines for the use of recycled building materials in City capital projects. 
•	Input into various policy and tender specification processes to ensure incorporation of green procurement principles. 
•	Completed a pilot for adopting green cleaning products at the City's Smart Living Centre. Based on the success of the project, it is planned to roll-out the initiative across directorates.
•	Supported and facilitated internal training and communication on the City's green procurement programme and Action Plan through workshops and presentations. 
•	Supported research on replacement of glyphosate used as an herbicide in City operations. 

Various partnerships are also in place since 2023 to support the implementation of the Green Procurement Action Plan. (EDP). Examples include:

•In 2023/24, the City completed a partnership project with GreenCape, for 'Technical support in the implementation of the City's Green Procurement Action Plan'. The project included workshops and other engagements, culminating in the finalisation of a set of 'Guidelines for Greening Large Capital Projects' and an accompanying framework/process-flow to mainstream greening of infrastructure projects. This is intended to support the City's Infrastructure Planning and Delivery Framework.

•In 2024/25 the City commenced a partnership project with the Economic Development Partnership, building on the GreenCape project mentioned above, intended to support green procurement in the Urban Mobility directorate's capital pipeline, as a basis/pilot for future engagement across other capital sectors. This project included multiple workshops, engagements and the development of a project steering committee and culminated in an action-learning report for greening urban mobility infrastructure. The approach and successful delivery of the intended outcomes of the 2024/25 project provides a strong basis to consolidate and expand the project and the partnership. The project team intends to focus on the Human Settlements Directorate within the 2025/26 project cycle.

•The City's Environmental Management Department continues to develop case studies of successful green procurement in projects and tenders and aims to publish these in the upcoming edition of the Mayor's Portfolio of Urban Sustainability (2026). 

•The City also continued its participation in regional, national and international green procurement initiatives and partnerships, including: collaboration with the Ellen MacArthur Foundation and ongoing engagement as a founding member of the Global Lead Cities Network on Sustainable Public Procurement.

column16: The City of Miami's Municipal Code (Chapter 22.5, Article III - Environmentally Preferable Purchasing) provides the framework to reduce negative impacts to human health and the environment through environmentally preferable purchasing in order to:(1) Increase purchases of environmentally preferable products and services to achieve the city's mission, while maintaining performance and availability and remaining cost effective, with continual improvement. (2) Reduce occupational health hazards for city staff and reduce exposure of city residents and visitors to potentially toxic chemicals by purchasing environmentally sensitive, sustainable goods for use, or identifying products to be used by service providers that do not harm human health or the environment. (3) Reduce the city's contribution to global climate change by purchasing goods and services that lead to a reduction in greenhouse gas emissions from commodities. (4) Improve the air quality for city residents and visitors by purchasing commodities that minimize emissions of air pollutants. (5) Protect the quality of the city's ground and surface waters by eliminating the use of chemicals known to contaminate local water resources and ecological systems through toxicity, bioaccumulation, or persistence. (6) Preserve resources locally and globally through purchasing practices that include: a. Maximizing the use of water and energy efficient products; b. Maximizing post-consumer recycled content and readily recyclable or compostable materials; c. Reducing the use or creation of landfilled materials; d. Favoring long-term product use through durability, repairability, and reuse; e. Considering life-cycle analysis of products consisting of, but not limited to, manufacture, transportation, use, and disposal; f. Supporting strong recycling markets; g. column16: The city has a sustainable purchasing policy that encourages the purchase of products and services for municipal operations that have a reduced effect on human health and the environment compared to competing products or services that serve the same purpose, while remaining fiscally responsible. Being fiscally responsible requires the City to consider full life cycle analysis of the cost of materials (this includes initial cost, transportation cost, energy cost, maintenance cost, replacement cost, disposal cost, and resale value). A consumption-based emissions inventory has been reported for the local food system and water system, with a full consumption based inventory to be completed once C40 Cities establishes related reporting protocols and requirements. Phoenix has been a member of C40's Consumption Based Emissions Workgroup along with other members across the world. Regarding implementation, the Phoenix City Council voted to transition the City's heavy-duty bus fleet to zero-emission models by 2040. Phoenix Public Transit provides transit service to about half of the Valley (the Phoenix metropolitan area), including local, commuter, and neighborhood circulator service. The department's fleet is currently made up of about 500 buses, which operate on compressed natural gas or diesel. Transit's zero emission work supports federal infrastructure modernization and implementation of local plans including the City of Phoenix's Climate Action Plan, Zero Emission Bus Plan, and Transportation Electrification Action Plan (https://www.phoenix.gov/content/dam/phoenix/sustainabilitysite/mediaassets/sustainability/ev-home-page-assets/City%20of%20PHX%20Transportation%20Electrification%20Action%20Plan.pdf). In August 2022, the Federal Transit Administration awarded the Phoenix Public Transit Department a $16.3 million grant for low- and no-emissions buses and supporting infrastructure. The grant is a catalyst for the department to begin transitioning its heavy-duty transit fleet to 100 percent zero-emission buses by 2040. Orders have been placed for 12 battery electric buses (BEB) through 2024, with the first pilot buses scheduled for delivery in 2025. The fleet transition will eventually operate up to 450 fuel cell electric and 50 BEBs. The infrastructure to fuel these 12 BEBs will be in place by the end of 2025. The Transportation Electrification Action Plan calls for investments in publicly available electric vehicle (EV) charging stations and micromobility solutions to promote residents' transition towards electric vehicle use, further reducing fuel consumption. The Transportation Electrification Action Plan, or EV roadmap, was approved by the Phoenix City Council in June of 2022. The City is transitioning its fleet to EVs, with a Phoenix Electric Vehicle implementation strategy goal of 200 EVs in the city fleet by 2030. There are 99 EVs in the city fleet as of summer 2025. The city is always looking for innovative solutions that will not only act as climate actions but also be fiscally responsible. The cool pavement program is one of those solutions, where a lighter colored coating is used on roadways to reduce the urban heat island effect. The City's Cool Pavement Program advanced out of the pilot phase in April 2023 into a full program within the pavement maintenance program, expanding to 11 locations. Phoenix reached its 100th mile of installed cool pavement in June 2023. The WTS Metropolitan Phoenix Chapter recognized the Cool Pavement Program for the 2022 Innovative Transportation Solutions Project of the Year award. One of the benefits of this work is that it appears the pavement will need to be replaced less frequently, reducing associated emissions. The City, in partnership with ASU, continues to evaluate cool pavement performance through scientific testing, resulting in findings that the cool pavement lasts twice as long as traditional blacktop (https://www.phoenix.gov/newsroom/street-transportation-department-news/3248.html).

Essa iniciativa tem como objetivo apoiar tanto os órgãos públicos quanto o setor privado no desenvolvimento de práticas mais sustentáveis.

column16:
With its Mannheim 2030 mission statement, the City of Mannheim has set itself the goal of promoting global justice and taking responsibility for environmentally and climate-friendly action. In order to meet this goal, the city administration weights social and ecological criteria in the procurement of goods and services with at least 30 percent (see V271/2022 - Ecologically and socially sustainable procurement at the city administration).
Procurement practice in Mannheim is thus already making a contribution to promoting fair trade, fair wages and working conditions as well as climate, environmental and resource protection, but must continue to be systematically expanded across all departments.

In 2023, new public tendering and award criteria were adopted for Mannheim daycare centers (crèche, kindergarten, after-school care) and schools. For example, the proportion of organic food components in lunchtime meals will be increased from the previous 40% to 50% of the total food input; dairy products and eggs will continue to be exclusively organic. The remaining required organic percentage can extend to product groups such as potatoes, pasta, rice, pulses, vegetables or salad. The use of fair trade quality products is also required. Selected convenience products will be deliberately avoided in future.

A new addition is the even better consideration of age-specific requirements for nursery catering in the form of a nursery-appropriate ovo-lacto-vegetarian menu line and a menu line with ovo-lacto-vegetarian food for nursery and after-school care. A balanced lunch supports educational success.

Further information can be found in the two draft resolutions V697/2022 and V103/2023.

column16: Malmö has an extensive ongoing work with sustainable and circular procurement. Since 2010 the purchasing of food has been monitored and the carbon emission from food decreased by 30% (baseline 1990), mainly by a shift to more plant based meals. Since 2019 the City has a contract for reused furniture (new contact began in 2023) which has led to about 200 tons less CO2-emissions per year. Over 20% of the office furniture bough be the city is reused. The city is incorporating transport criteria in all procurement where it is possible to lower the impact from transports. Circular criteria has also been broadly implemented in many procurements like ITC, signs, baby strollers, catering and single use products like plastics. During the year, a roadmap for the City of Malmö's work to achieve net-zero emissions has been developed. The goal of achieving net-zero emissions includes Scope 1-3 emissions. The roadmap is based on current knowledge about the transition area and focus on which measures are important to prioritize to achieve the goal of net-zero emissions. Firstly, the organization must utilize already existing resources that do not generate new emissions. Thereafter, products, materials, and services with the lowest possible climate impact are chosen. By making changes in procurement through, for example, setting requirements, as well as in purchasing behaviors and management, the organization can reduce its climate impact. Transitioning to a more circular system is fundamental for the organization to succeed in its ambitious goal. The roadmap work is carried out jointly across administrative boundaries, and the implementation of measures takes place within the departments. The roadmap is a tool to support that points out a common direction and helps us to prioritize. https://malmo.se/Om-Malmo-stad/Inkop-och-leverantorer/Upphandling-i-Malmo-stad/Malmo-stads-inkopspolicy.html

Procurement Manual 2025:
'Council's procurement activities will be carried out on the basis of obtaining Value for Money. This means minimising the total cost of ownership over the lifetime of the requirement consistent with acceptable quality, reliability and delivery considerations. Lowest price is not the sole determinant of Value for Money.
In assessing Value for Money, staff are responsible for giving due consideration to:
• Whole-of-life monetary cost, i.e.
o procurement price;
o operating and maintenance costs; and
o cost of environmentally responsible disposal or recycling/re-use/re-sale of the product;
• Non-monetary impacts (both negative and positive) over the life of the product or service; including
o environmental impacts;
o social impacts - particularly on marginalised or vulnerable people; and
o impacts on other Council priorities '

8. Sustainability & Social Procurement
Council is committed to procuring products and services in alignment with its values of environmental, social, economic and cultural sustainability. This section details the specific policy and operational implications of such considerations. Overall, tender documents or Requests for Quotation should contain:
• Clauses and weightings to assess environmental and social costs and benefits;
• Appropriately designed response statements to allow suppliers to clearly articulate how they will 
address social and environmental impacts; and
• Clauses that are framed as measurable deliverables rather than aspirations with regard to 
environmental, social, economic and cultural sustainability.
A pre-tender briefing could be used to explain the detail of such clauses, particularly if they refer to 
complex matters with which mainstream suppliers may not be familiar.

8.1 Environmental Sustainability
8.1.1 Sustainable procurement statement
Council is committed to addressing the climate emergency to the strongest degree possible. 
Council's adopted Climate Emergency Plan sets out our role in responding to this unprecedented 
challenge, and includes the following key objectives:
• achieve zero-net emissions across the entire Yarra community by 2030, and accelerate the removal of excess carbon emissions;
• activate our community to take effective climate action - pushing for urgent change and changing the way we live and work;
• ensure our community is safe, healthy and resilient - especially those most vulnerable to severe climate impacts;
• create a city that continues to adapt to a changing climate and is ecologically healthy for all species; and
• collaborate and advocate with others in the climate emergency movement to increase our impact.
Yarra Council was one of the first local governments in the world to declare a climate emergency, acknowledging both the scale and urgency of action needed to avoid the catastrophic impacts of global 
heating.
Effectively responding to the climate emergency requires transformational societal and economic 
change. It will require changing our resource intensive and high consuming ways of life, as well as adapting to living on a hotter planet. 
Procurement choices which respond proportionately to the climate emergency will contribute to the 
rapid reduction in carbon emissions in order to restore a safe climate. A key aspect of sustainable procurement is the application of circular economy principles (in which finite resources are valued and kept circulating within it) and lifecycle approaches to consider the full environmental impact of products and services, including embodied emissions. 

City of Yarra 
Council purchases environmentally preferable products and services whenever they meet Council's needs and are available at a competitive price. Council's sustainable procurement practices demonstrate to the community that Council is responding to the climate emergency at commensurate urgency and scale and supporting the circular economy by 
stimulating the market for environmentally preferable products.

Makati City incorporates green procurement principles and practices into its overall procurement processes and policies, aligning with national initiatives and global sustainability goals. This is achieved by integrating environmentally preferable criteria into the design and specifications of procurement projects, aiming for sustainable public procurement that considers the entire life cycle of goods and services. 

Here's a breakdown of how Makati City approaches green procurement:

1. Alignment with National Policies:

GPPB Roadmap:
Makati City's efforts are guided by the national Green Public Procurement (GPP) Roadmap, which aims to integrate sustainable practices into government procurement. Further, the New Government Procurement Act (NGPA), Republic Act No. 12009, promotes sustainable and green practices in government procurement. It aims to integrate environmental, social, and economic considerations into the design and implementation of government projects, minimizing negative environmental impacts and promoting long-term sustainability. 

Sources:
https://www.officialgazette.gov.ph/downloads/2025/02feb/20250210-IRR-RA-12009-FRM.pdf

https://www.gppb.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/GPP_roadmap_print.pdf

https://ngpa.gppb.gov.ph/New-Government-Procurement-Act-RA-12009.pdf

Sustainable Development Goals:
Makati's green procurement aligns with the broader Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly those related to environmental sustainability and responsible consumption and production. 

2. Key Aspects of Green Procurement in Makati:

Prioritizing Environmentally Friendly Products:
Makati City prioritizes purchasing goods and services that are energy-efficient, made from recycled materials, or have a lower carbon footprint. 

Life Cycle Assessment:
Procurement decisions consider the environmental impact of products from their creation to disposal, including factors like resource consumption, emissions, and waste generation. 

Promoting Green Markets:
By adopting green procurement practices, Makati City aims to drive market demand for sustainable products and services, encouraging businesses to develop more environmentally friendly solutions. 

Social and Economic Benefits:
Green procurement is recognized for its potential to improve public health, support fair labor practices, and promote local sourcing, contributing to positive social and economic outcomes. 

3. Specific Actions and Initiatives:
Technical Specifications:
Makati City incorporates green criteria into the technical specifications of procurement projects, ensuring that potential environmental impacts are considered. For example, city government packed meals should be:
- served on an Oxo-biodegradable container
- served with appropriate eco-friendly recyclable utensils, napkins and toothpicks
- drinks are served in eco-friendly recyclable paper cups (with at least 500ml consumption per serving).

Regular Updates of Green Product Lists:
The city collaborates with the Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System (PhilGEPS) to regularly publish and update lists of sustainable goods and services. 

Integration into Existing Frameworks:
Green procurement practices are being integrated into existing procurement processes rather than creating separate procedures. 

4. Examples of Green Procurement in Practice:
Energy Efficiency: Prioritizing energy-efficient appliances and equipment in government buildings and operations. For example, procurement of energy efficient appliances and office equipment such as AC unit, printers, photo copier machines, computers, etc. Higher stars as per DOE EEC rating.
Waste Reduction: Implementing measures to reduce waste generation and promote recycling and reuse. For example, the Paperless Policy of the City.
Sustainable Materials: Using eco-friendly materials in construction and other projects. For example, distribution and promotion of the use of tumblers.

5. Overall Goal:
The goal of green procurement in Makati City is to achieve value for money while minimizing environmental impact and contributing to a more sustainable future. By integrating green principles into its procurement practices, Makati City aims to lead by example and encourage wider adoption of sustainable practices across the public and private sectors.

New Taipei City has been responding to the 'Government Procurement Act' implemented by the central government since 1999, which stipulates that government agencies should give priority to purchasing environmentally friendly products. In 2006, the city formulated the 'Implementation Guidelines for Green Procurement by Government Agencies and Schools in New Taipei City,' which requires that the procurement ratio of eco-label products in designated categories should exceed 95% for all agencies and schools in the city. 

1.Promoting green procurement: In 2024, the total amount of green procurement exceeded NT$3.8 billion across various units: 
(1)Green procurement by government agencies: New Taipei City has established the 'Implementation Guidelines for Green Procurement by Government Agencies and Schools in New Taipei City,' which regulates and manages the green procurement performance of various agencies. The largest categories of procurement include photocopiers, toner cartridges, air conditioners, and office paper. 
(2) Promoting green procurement by private enterprises and organizations: Guidance is provided to encourage businesses, communities, and residents to prioritize the selection of products with green labels in their procurement processes. Public recognition and awards are given to encourage the involvement of businesses or private organizations. For example, 'Taiwan Cement Corporation Taipei Cement Plant' purchases cement raw materials with environmental labels to reduce environmental impact. 'Cheng Loong Corp.' has been continuously purchasing pulp that is environmentally friendly and certified by FSC. 

2.Assisting service providers in transitioning to low-carbon operations: Guidance is provided to help businesses transform their products or services into low-carbon alternatives. This includes the following two aspects: 
(1) Assisting restaurants in not providing disposable tableware proactively, prioritizing the use of seasonal local ingredients, and promoting food waste reduction, thus becoming eco-friendly restaurants. 
(2) Assisting service-oriented businesses in applying for environmental labels if they have the potential, such as hotels, travel agencies, or recreational venues. This encourages them to reduce carbon emissions and waste in their operations, management, and facilities. 

3.Promoting green consumption to the public: The city government collaborates with businesses, community organizations, civic activities, and other counties and cities to organize online or offline events that promote the concept of green living to the public. This includes concepts such as sharing, renting instead of buying, sustainable consumption, and second-hand exchanges. The aim is to encourage people to change their consumption habits and stimulate businesses to provide green products and services. 

Link: 
1. New Taipei Achieves NT$3.8B in Green Procurement with Joint Efforts Toward Sustainability
https://www.epd.ntpc.gov.tw/Article/Info?ID=11813

2.The Environmental Protection Administration Green Procurement Website: https://greenlifestyle.moenv.gov.tw/greenPurChase 

The New Taipei City government has established the 'New Taipei City Climate Change Response Action Autonomy Ordinance (Draft),' which is currently under legislative review. The ordinance includes provisions aimed at reducing consumption emissions, as outlined below: 
1. Public works within the city's jurisdiction should prioritize planning, design, construction, and use of waste resource products as materials or additives. 
2. The tourism and hotel industries within the city's jurisdiction are prohibited from providing disposable items for free and should actively promote consumers bringing their own non-disposable items. 
3. Designated public and private dining establishments in New Taipei City are prohibited from providing disposable utensils for dine-in customers and should offer incentives for takeout customers who bring their own containers. 
4. Designated public and private establishments should establish a circulating system for borrowing, returning, and cleaning reusable containers (referred to as 'circular containers'). 
5. E-commerce platforms designated by the New Taipei City government, when selling goods to the city, should use environmentally friendly packaging and shock-resistant materials. 
6. Plastic shopping bags sold by designated public and private establishments should be dual-purpose bags that can also be used as garbage bags, as produced by the city government. 
7. Designated public and private establishments should implement measures or facilities for reducing and reusing food waste. 
8. Government agencies, schools, and designated businesses within the city's jurisdiction should implement green procurement and use products certified with environmental labels, water and energy-saving labels, green building materials, carbon labels, or carbon reduction labels.

column16:
Bacolod City, with its strategic location on Negros Island (often called the 'Renewable Energy Capital of the Philippines'), has been taking significant steps to promote and implement renewable energy initiatives. These efforts are driven by the goals of reducing electricity costs, enhancing energy security, and contributing to national and global climate change mitigation.

Here are some of Bacolod's key initiatives and projects in renewable energy:

1. Solarization of Government Buildings: The most prominent initiative is the installation of solar photovoltaic (PV) systems on government buildings. This is a flagship program under the current city administration.

I. Solar Energy Projects
a. Bacolod City Government Center (BCGC): A 400-kilowatt (KW) solar system has been installed and is operational on the rooftop of the BCGC. This project is expected to generate significant cost savings for the city government.

https://bacolodcity.gov.ph/bcgs-launches-solar-power-system/

b. Barangay-level Installations: The city has been rolling out solar power installations in public buildings across several barangays. These projects, with a total capacity of 1,340 KW, are projected to reduce the electricity bills of participating barangays by as much as 50%. This not only saves money but also promotes the use of clean energy at the grassroots level.

https://bacolodcity.gov.ph/mabbs-solar-energy-project-in-bacolod-city/

2. Bacolod Solar Power Project: Nexif Ratch Energy, a major independent power producer, has developed a 145 MWp (megawatt-peak) ground-mounted solar project that spans parts of Bacolod and nearby Bago City. This utility-scale project is a significant contributor to the grid's renewable energy supply.

https://nexifratch.com/project/negros-ph-solar-inc/

II. Establishment of Local Energy Code
In line with national laws, the Bacolod City Sangguniang Panlungsod (City Council) has approved a 'Local Energy Code.' This ordinance is crucial for Policy and Regulation and for Facilitating Projects. 

https://bacolodcity.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/CO-1044.pdf

III. Electric Vehicles (E-Jeepneys)
Bacolod has also been at the forefront of the country's public transport modernization program. The city has introduced electric jeepneys (e-jeepneys) to its public transport system. This move supports a transition away from fossil fuels, reducing air pollution and the city's carbon footprint.

https://bacolodcity.gov.ph/launching-of-electric-jeepneys-at-bcgc-lobby/

Dundee City Council's Corporate Procurement Strategy 2024-2027 outlines several specific actions aimed at reducing emissions through procurement. These actions are embedded within a broader sustainability and community wealth building agenda. Here are the key initiatives:

Dundee City Council is developing tailored strategies for major procurement categories such as construction, ICT, and fleet. These strategies will assess how carbon emissions are generated—either through manufacturing or logistics—and create action plans to reduce them. This includes changing what is bought and localising supply chains to cut transport-related emissions, aligning with community wealth building goals.

Sustainability is embedded in every procurement specification. The Council uses Scottish Government tools to identify environmental risks and opportunities, such as reducing carbon emissions, promoting recycling, and avoiding hazardous materials. Suppliers are encouraged to use net zero toolkits, with links provided in tender documents to support their sustainability efforts.

The Council has measured Scope 3 emissions—those generated by suppliers—and identified high-emission categories. These will be addressed through category strategies that promote circular economy principles, extend asset life, and assess purchases based on whole life costs rather than upfront price alone.

Procurement specifications are outcome-based, allowing suppliers to propose sustainable delivery methods. All significant contracts include community benefit clauses, and a new Community Wish List initiative enables suppliers to deliver small-scale environmental or social projects as part of their contractual obligations.

To track progress, the Council has set key performance indicators. One target is to develop three category strategies addressing Scope 3 emissions and local opportunities in the first year, increasing to ten by year three. These strategies will be monitored through annual procurement reports.

column16: Cornwall Council is committed to ensuring that we deliver procurement in a responsible way. The Responsible Procurement policy was updated in April 2021 and sets out our principles to ensure that the council follows the general principles to deliver value for money, meet the needs of residents and achieve additional economic, social and environmental benefits. The Council incorporates value for money of the goods, services and works it procures, reducing our carbon emissions, ethical sourcing and compliance with legislation within our responsible procurement policy. We are also drafting a Supply Chain Decarbonisation Strategy at the moment, set to be introduced in 2026. It is designed to specifically target emissions associated with the goods, works and services the Council purchases and will promote positive impacts wherever practical, and look at whole life costs of delivery. A large proportion of Cornwall's total emissions are outside of our direct control but within our influence, and this includes emissions from our supply chain. Our aim is to facilitate local leadership to influence the action of our partners and suppliers through leveraging the Council's purchasing power to get suppliers to reduce carbon emissions as a competitive part of the tendering process. This will foster a more self-reliant, sustainable and diverse local supply chain. All procurements in scope will require a relevant focus on reducing carbon emissions, which will be monitored inc. vehicle emissions, energy use, embodied carbon within materials and products and planning for a changing environment. The principles of the new Strategy have already been trialled in several procurement and commissioning exercises including with our Homecare provision contract, emissions reductions there focusing on reducing carbon-intensive travel. In addition, in order to support the Council's own service design process category guidance was produced to help to embed targeted carbon objectives within our sourcing process. The documents covered 8 sourcing categories and subcategories and detail specific interventions for each.

column16: The WMCA uses the Social Value Portal's TOMs Framework to maximise social value (including carbon reduction) generation from its procurement activity. In 2023, the WMCA convened public sector partners in a task and finish group to outline a regional approach to the decarbonisation of procured goods and services. In 2024 the WMCA conducted a scope 3 carbon assessment of its own scope 3 footprint which provided the organisation with a scope 3 carbon baseline, and highlighted particular areas of the organisation's scope 3 footprint to focus on. As a result of this work the WMCA is currently in the process of developing and implementing an ambitious approach to managing the decarbonisation of its procurement activity. Additionally, the WMCA is commit to embedding a more deliberate and socially purposeful model of economic growth - measured not only by how fast or aggressive it is; but also, by how well it is created and shared across the whole population and place, and by the social and environmental outcomes it realises for our people. This is the West Midlands Combined Authority definition of Inclusive Growth. Inclusive Growth is largely about recognising the wider impacts that a project has or could have beyond its primary aims, outputs and outcomes. Inclusive Growth has eight fundamentals which officers are asked to consider when developing an intervention. To support the embedding of Inclusive Growth across the organisation, the WMCA has developed an Inclusive Growth Implementation Toolkit (ITK). The ITK is a self-service survey-based toolkit for members of staff which provides tailored feedback on how well projects align with the eight fundamentals of Inclusive Growth. The ITK also provides recommendations for how to boost the alignment of the project. The ITK has been developed to be used at the design, decision making and evaluation stage of the development of all projects. This supports officers in reducing emissions from their project's procurement and purchase of goods and services, as well as the broader emissions associated with projects.\n

This Sustainable Procurement Policy has been developed in line with the
three Tayside Councils key Procurement Strategy and in response to the
Scottish Government's Sustainable Procurement Action Plan. The aim of the
Sustainable Procurement Policy is to embed sustainable development
principles (social, economic and environmental) into all procurement within
the three Councils and Tayside Contracts.

Our key sustainability objectives
Sustainable procurement can offer whole life cost efficiency, supports our
commitment to Corporate Social Responsibility, evidences that we are a
responsible public body and can promote health improvements amongst all
our stakeholders.
The Council will, through their procurement activities and using appropriate
and effective evaluation techniques, strive to:
 Promote use of local products and services
 Create job opportunities for local people, and increase the number
of apprentices in employment
 Engage effectively with the third sector and SMEs
 Influence the supply chain to promote sustainable procurement
 Reduce greenhouse gas emissions and mitigate the impacts of
Climate Change
 Increase our use of renewable energy and energy efficient products
 Increase the percentage of reused, recycled and sustainable or
ethically sourced materials, resources and products
 Reduce the percentage of waste to landfill

The Council's Climate Change Strategy and Action Plan also includes a number of Governance related actions to reduce emissions from purchased goods and services. These include:
Action G2 - Mainstream climate change into committee procedures and council operations
Action G8 - Ensure climate change considerations are embedded at the outset of and during the life cycle of strategic planning process.
Action G10 - Develop tool for whole life carbon decision making
Action G12 - Identifying a climate change champion in each Service or key Team
Action G14 - Reduce unnecessary end of year IT purchasing though December 31 spend ban

In 2022, H&F adopted a low carbon procurement policy establishing general principles for H&F to follow across all our procurement and commissioning activities: https://democracy.lbhf.gov.uk/documents/s119810/WLA%20low-carbon%20procurement%20policy.pdf

We developed this in collaboration with other boroughs in west London to ensure a consistent approach across the sub-region. The policy is accompanied by a charter for suppliers to sign and a toolkit for officers to use during the tender stage. The toolkit is a self-assessment to help officers think about how their projects, procurements, commissioning, and services align with H&F's net zero carbon target. The charter asks suppliers to set out actions they will take to reduce their organisation's carbon emissions. Both documents encourage procurement officers and account managers to embed climate considerations during the tender stage.

Furthermore, all procurement decision reports and strategies require the author to consider and include Climate Implications, which are signed off by a senior member of the climate team. Decision reports, a key aspect of the council's governance processes, set out the details, reasoning and impacts of a proposed decision or project. Finalised reports are reviewed by Cabinet members and other senior officials before a decision is made. All decision reports setting out procurement strategies require the inclusion of Climate Implications, which officers should determine using a dedicated Climate Implications Toolkit: https://democracy.lbhf.gov.uk/documents/s122999/Appendix%204.pdf 
This seeks to ensure that climate change impacts are considered when the council procures goods and services.

The Metropolitan Council is committed to reducing operational emissions with the goal of carbon neutrality through multiple strategies, including making buildings more energy efficient, purchasing and generating renewable energy, transitioning government fleets to electric and alternative fuel vehicles, and attempting energy and resource recovery from wastewater treatment. 

The Met Council reports annually to the Minnesota Office of Enterprise Sustainability about our procurement practices. We procure pool fleet vehicles through the state cooperative contract, in which we are required to purchase electric or hybrid vehicles if they can fulfill the purpose of the vehicle and only purchase internal combustion vehicles if a reasonable EV or hybrid is not available. 

The Council also has a program to procure used products. Metro Transit has a refurbish and vendor exchange program in place and has found significant sustainability savings by refurbishing in house or having outside vendors rebuild and repair unserviceable parts. Our Wastewater Treatment plants utilize auctions to buy products and will also auction items to be reused instead of being trashed. 

In terms of office supplies and janitorial products, the Council purchases paper that is certified by the Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) or the Sustainability Forestry Initiative (SFI) and is at least 30% recycled. Our vendor Toshiba provides high-yield toners for all devices. The Council also purchases janitorial paper products that are certified by the Sustainability Forestry Initiative (SFI).

The 10 Local Authorities that make up the City Region, along with other public bodies such as Health Boards are annually reporting consumption emissions using the Welsh Government guidance and methodology. Work is ongoing to both improved reporting methodologies to ensure reductions in emissions from PG&S can be captured and dedicated efforts with supply chains to reduce emissions are acknowledged.
As a statutory public body, CCR CJC are also preparing their own operational carbon footprint this year to report into Welsh Government for the FY25 period. This includes an assessment of Purchased Goods and Services. The annual (voluntary) public sector reporting categories required by Welsh Government include; Scope 1, 2 and 3 (Purchased goods and services, business travel, staff commuting, waste and water).
The footprint prepared for FY25 will form the basis of a Carbon Reduction Plan for Cardiff Capital Regions own activities, including engagement with suppliers to reduce the impact of emissions from purchased goods and services.

Skellefteå municipality has an established goal to reduce emissions from procurement through its Environmental and Climate Programme, specifically Milestone Goal 2: 'Use procurement for efficient resource use and reduced environmental and climate impact.' This goal aims to minimize hazardous substances in procured goods, services, and contracts, and to increase the share of circular purchases.

To support this, the municipality has implemented a sustainability analysis for all investments over SEK 20 million, where climate impacts during both construction and operational phases must be addressed. This ensures that emission reductions are considered early in procurement and investment planning.

A comprehensive climate analysis shows that indirect emissions from procurement, particularly construction and service contracts, constitute the majority of municipal emissions. Therefore, reducing emissions from purchased goods and services is a strategic priority in achieving Skellefteå's climate neutrality goal by 2030.
